The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

Assume AC and a parametric model QMD at $\theta_0$ with score $s_{\theta_0}$.
Then
$$E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}=0,$$
and the information matrix
$I_{\theta_0}=E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$ has finite entries
and is positive semidefinite. The QMD convention and square-integrability of
the score are those of [[def-qmd-path]].

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[def-qmd-path]]. Write $p_0=p_{\theta_0}$,
$p_u=p_{\theta_0+u}$, and $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$. Let
$$\alpha(u):=P_{\theta_0+u}(p_0=0),\qquad \beta(u):=P_0(p_u=0).$$
Then $\alpha(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$ and $\beta(u)=o(\|u\|_2^2)$ as $u\to0$.

If $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ are IID real random variables and $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, then, with $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|\longrightarrow0.$$
Consequently $S_n/n\to\mu$ in probability.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

If $X_n\to X$ in $L^1$ on a probability space, then
$\{X,X_0,X_1,\ldots\}$ is uniformly integrable.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_C)}{\iota(n!)}(x-\xi_C)^n(x-a).$$

derivations.claim: Write $p_u=p_{\theta_0+u}$, $S=\{p_0>0\}$, and $\alpha(u)=\int_{S^c}p_u\,d\mu$. For small $u$, [F3] gives $\alpha(u)<1/2$. Define $q_u=\mathbf1_Sp_u/((1-\alpha(u))p_0)$ on $S$ and $q_u=0$ on $S^c$. It is nonnegative and measurable, and $\int q_u\,dP_0=(1-\alpha(u))^{-1}\int_Sp_u\,d\mu=1,$ so it is a probability density. At $u=0$, $\alpha(0)=0$ and $q_0=1$ $P_0$-almost surely, since $P_0(S^c)=\int_{S^c}p_0\,d\mu=0$. On $S$, $\sqrt{q_u}=(1-\alpha(u))^{-1/2} \left(1+\tfrac12u^Ts+\frac{r_u}{\sqrt{p_0}}\right).$ The residual term has $L^2(P_0)$ norm $\|r_u\mathbf1_S\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(\|u\|_2)$. Also $|(1-\alpha)^{-1/2}-1| =\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{1-\alpha}(1+\sqrt{1-\alpha})}=O(\alpha),$ and [F2], [F8] give $\|u^Ts\|_{L^2(P_0)}=O(\|u\|_2)$. Therefore $Y_u:=2(\sqrt{q_u}-1)=u^Ts+R_u, \qquad\|R_u\|_{L^2(P_0)}=o(\|u\|_2).$ This is the required square-root expansion.

The product function $L_n=\prod_iq_{u_n}(X_i)$ is a density of $\bar P_n^{\otimes n}$ relative to $P_0^{\otimes n}$. For a measurable rectangle $A_1\times\cdots\times A_n$, Tonelli gives $\int_{A_1\times\cdots\times A_n}\prod_iq_{u_n}(x_i)\,dP_0^{\otimes n} =\prod_i\int_{A_i}q_{u_n}\,dP_0 =\prod_i\bar P_n(A_i).$ By [F6], agreement on rectangles identifies the product measures. Taking the whole space gives $E_{P_0^{\otimes n}}L_n=1$.

Since $E_0q_u=1$, $E_0Y_u=-\tfrac14E_0Y_u^2.$ By step 1.1, [F2], and [F8], $E_0Y_u^2=u^TIu+o(\|u\|_2^2),\qquad E_0Y_u=-\tfrac14u^TIu+o(\|u\|_2^2).$ Indeed, the difference between $Y_u$ and $u^Ts$ has $L^2(P_0)$ norm $o(\|u\|_2)$, so Cauchy–Schwarz makes the difference of their squared norms $o(\|u\|_2^2)$.

Apply [F4] to $Z_i=\|s(X_i)\|_2^2$, whose mean is finite by [F2]. Then $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(h_n^Ts(X_i))^2\to h^TIh$ in probability: for fixed $h$ this is [F4] applied to $(h^Ts)^2$, and the difference for $h_n$ is bounded by $\|h_n-h\|_2\|h_n+h\|_2\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|s(X_i)\|_2^2\to0.$ Step 1.1 and [F8] also give $\sum_{i=1}^nY_{u_n}(X_i)^2 -\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(h_n^Ts(X_i))^2\to0$ in probability, because its expected absolute value is at most $n\|R_{u_n}\|_2(\|Y_{u_n}\|_2+\|u_n^Ts\|_2) =o(n\|u_n\|_2^2)=o(1)$. Consequently $\sum_iY_{u_n}(X_i)^2\to h^TIh$.

Put $V_n=\sqrt nY_{u_n}(X_1)$. Step 1.1 implies $V_n-h_n^Ts(X_1)\to0$ in $L^2(P_0)$, so $V_n\to h^Ts(X_1)$ in $L^2$. By [F8], $V_n^2\to(h^Ts(X_1))^2$ in $L^1$; [F9] makes $(V_n^2)$ uniformly integrable. For every $\varepsilon>0$, [F10] and the union bound give $P_0^{\otimes n}\!\left(\max_{i\le n}|Y_{u_n}(X_i)|>\varepsilon\right) \le\varepsilon^{-2}E_0[V_n^2\mathbf1_{\{|V_n|>\varepsilon\sqrt n\}}] \to0.$ Also $P_0^{\otimes n}(L_n=0)\le n\beta(u_n)\to0$ by [F3] and the union bound.

Let $R_{u_n}=Y_{u_n}-u_n^Ts$. Its centered IID sum has variance at most $nE_0R_{u_n}^2=o(n\|u_n\|_2^2)=o(1)$. By step 2.1, $nE_0R_{u_n}=nE_0Y_{u_n} =-\tfrac14h_n^TIh_n+o(1)\to-\tfrac14h^TIh.$ Markov's inequality [F10], applied to the square of the centered sum, gives $\sum_iY_{u_n}(X_i)=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac14h^TIh+o_P(1).$ This is the required expansion of the sum.

On the event that every $q_{u_n}(X_i)>0$ and $\max_i|Y_{u_n}(X_i)|\le1$, Taylor's formula gives $\log q_{u_n}(X_i)=Y_{u_n}(X_i)-\tfrac14Y_{u_n}(X_i)^2 +O(|Y_{u_n}(X_i)|^3),$ with one constant valid for all $i,n$ by [F11], since the third derivative of $y\mapsto2\log(1+y/2)$ is bounded on $[-1,1]$. The total cubic remainder is bounded by a constant times $\max_i|Y_{u_n}(X_i)|\sum_iY_{u_n}(X_i)^2$, which tends to zero by the square-sum limit in step 2.2 and the maximum bound in step 2.3. Combining the sum expansion in step 3.1 with the square-sum limit gives $\log L_n=\sum_i\log q_{u_n}(X_i) =h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1).$ This is the normalized log-likelihood expansion.

The full one-observation law decomposes as $P_{u_n}=(1-\alpha_n)\bar P_n+\alpha_n S_n$, where $S_n$ is the normalized restriction of $P_{u_n}$ to $S^c$ when $\alpha_n>0$. In the product mixture, the probability that at least one coordinate is drawn from $S_n$ is at most $n\alpha_n$. Conditioning on the all-absolutely-continuous component shows, for every event, its probability under the full product differs from that under $\bar P_n^{\otimes n}$ by at most $n\alpha_n$. Since $n\alpha_n=o(n\|u_n\|_2^2)=o(1)$, [F7] proves the total-variation claim. If $\alpha_n=0$, the singular component is absent and the same bound is zero.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P_{n,h}$ be probability laws on a common measurable space for each
integer $n\ge1$ and local parameter $h\in\mathbb R^d$, where $d<\infty$ and
$P_{n,0}$ is the base law. Suppose that for every fixed $h$ we are supplied a
nonnegative measurable function $L_{n,h}$ with
$$\int L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}=1.$$
It defines an absolutely continuous proxy
$$\bar P_{n,h}(A):=\int_A L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}.$$
The actual local law is allowed to have a singular part; the approximation
condition below is what connects it to this proxy.

The experiments are **locally asymptotically normal (LAN)** at $h=0$ with
information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$ if $K$ is a symmetric
positive semidefinite $d\times d$ matrix, $\Delta_n$ is an $\mathbb R^d$-valued
statistic,
$$\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)\quad\text{under }P_{n,0},$$
and for every fixed $h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\|P_{n,h}-\bar P_{n,h}\|_{\rm TV}\to0,\qquad \log L_{n,h}=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TKh+o_{P_{n,0}}(1),$$
where $\|\cdot\|_{\rm TV}$ is the event-supremum total variation distance
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]) and
$o_{P_{n,0}}(1)$ means convergence to zero in $P_{n,0}$-probability. We set
$\log0=-\infty$; the finite-valued expansion entails
$P_{n,0}(L_{n,h}=0)\to0$. Convergence in distribution is as in
[[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], and $N_d(0,K)$ allows
singular $K$ ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

If $P_{n,h}=\bar P_{n,h}$, this is the usual dominated LAN comparison. The
proxy formulation also covers QMD paths whose local alternatives are not
absolutely continuous with respect to the base law, provided the singular
product mass tends to zero in total variation. This definition is pointwise
in each fixed $h$; it does not assert uniformity over bounded sets of $h$.

Assume AC. In a pointwise LAN experiment [[def-lan-experiment]] with $K\succ0$, fix $h_1,\ldots,h_s\in\mathbb R^d$ and weights $w_i>0$ summing to one. Let $g:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Lipschitz. The Bayes values for estimating $h$ with loss $g(a-h)$ and this finite prior, allowing all measurable randomized rules, converge to the corresponding Bayes value in the Gaussian shift $Y\mid h\sim N_d(h,K^{-1})$. No likelihood-field uniformity or measurable-selection hypothesis is required.

Assume AC. Let $Q_h=N_d(h,S)$ with $S\succ0$ and let $g:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ have Lipschitz constant $B<\infty$. For every Borel probability prior $\pi$ on $\mathbb R^d$ and $\epsilon>0$, there is a finite-support prior $\pi_f$ whose Bayes value for loss $g(a-h)$ differs from that of $\pi$ by less than $\epsilon$. The comparison is uniform over all measurable randomized rules. In particular this applies to every diffuse Gaussian prior; no posterior selector assumption is needed.

Assume AC. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable, symmetric and quasi-convex, with $M>0$. For integers $N\ge2$ and $m\ge1$, put $\delta=M/N$, $C_k=\overline{\{x:L(x)\le k\delta\}}$ and
$$g_{N,m}(x)=\delta\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\min(1,m\,d(x,C_k)).$$
For $C_k=\varnothing$ the corresponding summand is defined to be one, and for $C_k=\mathbb R^d$ it is zero. Then $0\le g_{N,m}\le L$, and $g_{N,m}$ is bounded and Lipschitz. For every nondegenerate Gaussian $H\sim N_d(b,S)$,
$$\inf_a E g_{N,m}(a-H)=E g_{N,m}(H-b),\qquad \lim_{N\to\infty}\lim_{m\to\infty}E g_{N,m}(H-b)=E L(H-b).$$
Each summand is symmetric and quasi-convex; no quasi-convexity of their sum is asserted.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable
parameter and data spaces, with $\Theta$ nonempty, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel, writing
$P_\theta=K(\theta,\cdot)$ for the sampling law
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). Let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a nonempty measurable action space
([[def-measurable-space]]). Let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to\overline{\mathbb R}$
be measurable from the product measurable space with sigma-algebra
$\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal G$ to the extended real line with its Borel
sigma-algebra, and assume $L(\theta,a)\geq0$ for all $(\theta,a)$
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], [[def-extended-reals]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra-on-the-extended-real-line]]). A **prior** $\pi$ is a
probability measure on $\Theta$. The risk function $\theta\mapsto R(\theta,\delta)$ is measurable
under these hypotheses by kernel integration
([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]],
[[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The **Bayes risk** of
$\delta$ under $\pi$ is
$$r_\pi(\delta)=\int_\Theta R(\theta,\delta)\,\pi(d\theta)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Its **worst-case risk** is
$$R^*(\delta)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta,\delta)\in[0,+\infty],$$
and the **minimax value** is
$$V_{\rm mm}=\inf\{R^*(\delta):\delta\text{ is a measurable randomized rule from data to actions}\}\in[0,+\infty].$$
These suprema and infima are taken in the extended order on $\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]]); they exist by
[[lem-extended-reals-complete]]. The parameter set is nonempty and the rule
class is nonempty under the action-space hypothesis, so these are suprema and
infima of nonempty sets of nonnegative extended risks.
A rule is minimax if its worst-case risk equals this infimum. These definitions
make no assertion that a minimizer exists. Nonemptiness of $\mathsf D$ ensures
the rule class is nonempty: fixing any $a_0\in\mathsf D$ gives the constant
point-mass rule $x\mapsto\delta_{a_0}$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]), so
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]] makes
$\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ a sigma-algebra. Let $n,m\in\mathbb N$ with
$n,m \ge 1$.

- A function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is **Borel measurable** when
  it is measurable as a map

  $$f : (\mathbb{R}^n,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)) \to (\mathbb{R}^m,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^m))$$

  in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

- A function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is **Lebesgue measurable** when
  it is measurable as a map

  $$f : (\mathbb{R}^n,\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)) \to (\mathbb{R}^m,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^m)),$$

  where $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is the Lebesgue sigma-algebra of
  [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]].

When $m=1$, these are the corresponding notions for real-valued functions.

derivations.claim: If $M=0$, then $L$ is identically zero and the claimed bound is equality. Assume $M>0$ for the rest of the proof. Fix arbitrary integers $N\ge2$ and $m\ge1$, and set $g=g_{N,m}$ from [F4]; it is bounded Lipschitz and $g\le L$. For each $\rho>0$, set $\Gamma=\rho^{-1}K^{-1}$, and let $\pi_\Gamma=N_d(0,\Gamma)$. Define $V_{n,c}(g)=\inf_{\widehat h_n}\sup_{\|h\|_2\le c} E_{P_{n,h}}g(\widehat h_n-h)$ and $V(g)=\liminf_{c\to\infty}\liminf_{n\to\infty}V_{n,c}(g)$. If a finite prior $\pi_f$ is supported in the radius-$c$ ball, then every worst-case risk is at least its prior average by [F5]. Taking infima gives $V_{n,c}(g)\ge B_n(\pi_f,g)$, the finite-prior Bayes value.

In the Gaussian shift, $Y\mid h\sim N_d(h,K^{-1})$. Multiplying its likelihood by the prior density $N_d(0,\Gamma)$ and completing the square gives $H\mid Y\sim N_d(SK Y,S),\qquad S=(K+\Gamma^{-1})^{-1}.$ For the fixed constructed loss $g=g_{N,m}$, [F4] gives that the posterior risk is minimized at $SKY$, with value $E g(N_d(0,S))$ independent of $Y$. The action $Y\mapsto SKY$ is measurable and attains this value, so $B_G(\pi_\Gamma,g)=E g(N_d(0,S))$.

Let $C_f=\max\{\|h\|_2:h\in\operatorname{supp}(\pi_f)\}$. For every $c\ge C_f$, [F2] gives $B_n(\pi_f,g)\to B_G(\pi_f,g)$, where $B_G$ is the Bayes value in the Gaussian shift. Hence $V(g)\ge B_G(\pi_f,g)$. Since this holds for every finite prior, the bound also holds for any value approximated by finite-prior Bayes values.

For every $\eta>0$, [F3] supplies a finite prior $\pi_f$ whose Gaussian-shift Bayes value differs from $B_G(\pi_\Gamma,g)$ by less than $\eta$. Step 2.2 therefore gives $V(g)\ge B_G(\pi_\Gamma,g)-\eta$. Let $\eta\downarrow0$ to obtain $V(g)\ge B_G(\pi_\Gamma,g)$.

Here $S=(1+\rho)^{-1}K^{-1}$. Couple $N_d(0,S)$ as $(1+\rho)^{-1/2}Z$ for $Z\sim N_d(0,K^{-1})$. If $B_g$ is a Lipschitz constant for $g$, then $\left|E g((1+\rho)^{-1/2}Z)-E g(Z)\right| \le B_g\left(1-(1+\rho)^{-1/2}\right)E\|Z\|_2\to0$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ by [F7]. By steps 3.1 and 2.1, for each $\rho>0$ we have $V(g)\ge E g((1+\rho)^{-1/2}Z)$. Since the construction applies for every $\rho>0$, taking $\rho\downarrow0$ yields $V(g)\ge E g(Z)$.

Since $g\le L$, every estimator's risk under $L$ dominates its risk under this fixed $g$, so the local minimax value for $L$ is at least $V(g)$. Step 4.1 gives the lower bound $E g_{N,m}(Z)$. The choices $N,m$ in step 1.1 were arbitrary; first let $m\to\infty$ and then $N\to\infty$. By [F4] these lower bounds converge to $E L(Z)$. This is the stated inequality.

boundaries.reason: The local experiment supplies a probability law at each h and K is positive definite in dimension d>=1. Every radius-c parameter ball contains zero, and constant estimators give a nonempty rule class.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 treats M=0, when both sides are zero.

Statement and Proof: In scalar dimension the Gaussian lower benchmark has variance 1/K. Point-mass residual decision rules and finite one-atom priors are allowed in the infimum and comparison, while the eventual diffuse prior supplies the strong bound.

boundaries.reason: Statement assumes K positive definite so K^{-1} exists.

boundaries.evidence: M=0 is explicitly handled in step 1.1 with identically zero loss and equality. The Gaussian-prior parameter rho is positive during inversion and tends downward to zero only through the Lipschitz expectation limit in step 4.1.

The theorem assumes AC for Gaussian suppliers. Finite-prior comparisons use the constructive rational-grid rule of F2; the diffuse Gaussian posterior center SKY in step 2.1 is an explicit measurable action.

boundaries.reason: Finite-prior LAN convergence, diffuse Gaussian comparisons and Lipschitz minorants give the bowl-loss Gaussian lower bound in step 5.1.
An estimator meeting the lower bound does not imply that its experiment is LAN, and the theorem is a lower inequality rather than an efficiency equivalence.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed quantifier/limit order: fix one Lipschitz minorant and finite prior before n tends to infinity; finite support fits every sufficiently large c, so the minimax infimum is bounded by convergent finite-prior Bayes values. Finite-prior approximation then transfers the diffuse Gaussian prior bound. Gaussian posterior completion gives mean SKY and covariance (K+Gamma^{-1})^{-1}; centering is supplied for this minorant sum. Letting rho decrease to zero uses finite Gaussian first moment and Lipschitz g, then m tends to infinity before N via the minorant lemma. No estimator regularity, compact-uniform LAN or parameter-measurable full experiment is required for finite-prior inequalities. M=0 is explicit; K positive definite is essential. No defect found; no edits.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

Assume AC and [[def-qmd-path]] at $\theta_0$ with score $s$ and information $I$.
Let $h_n\to h$ in $\mathbb R^d$, put $u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$, and write
$P_0=P_{\theta_0}$ and $P_{u_n}=P_{\theta_0+u_n}$. On
$S=\{p_{\theta_0}>0\}$ define, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$q_n(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_S(x)p_{\theta_0+u_n}(x)} {(1-\alpha_n)p_{\theta_0}(x)},\qquad \alpha_n=P_{u_n}(S^c).$$
Then $q_n$ is a probability density relative to $P_0$. For IID
$X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, let $L_n=\prod_{i=1}^nq_n(X_i)$ and
$\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)$. Under $P_0^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad P_0^{\otimes n}(L_n=0)\to0.$$
Moreover, if $\bar P_n=q_nP_0$ is the normalized absolutely continuous
component of $P_{u_n}$ relative to $P_0$, then
$$\|P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}-\bar P_n^{\otimes n}\|_{\rm TV}\to0.$$
No full likelihood ratio for $P_{u_n}^{\otimes n}$ is asserted.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Let $P_{n,h}$ be probability laws on a common measurable space for each
integer $n\ge1$ and local parameter $h\in\mathbb R^d$, where $d<\infty$ and
$P_{n,0}$ is the base law. Suppose that for every fixed $h$ we are supplied a
nonnegative measurable function $L_{n,h}$ with
$$\int L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}=1.$$
It defines an absolutely continuous proxy
$$\bar P_{n,h}(A):=\int_A L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}.$$
The actual local law is allowed to have a singular part; the approximation
condition below is what connects it to this proxy.

The experiments are **locally asymptotically normal (LAN)** at $h=0$ with
information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$ if $K$ is a symmetric
positive semidefinite $d\times d$ matrix, $\Delta_n$ is an $\mathbb R^d$-valued
statistic,
$$\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)\quad\text{under }P_{n,0},$$
and for every fixed $h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\|P_{n,h}-\bar P_{n,h}\|_{\rm TV}\to0,\qquad \log L_{n,h}=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TKh+o_{P_{n,0}}(1),$$
where $\|\cdot\|_{\rm TV}$ is the event-supremum total variation distance
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]) and
$o_{P_{n,0}}(1)$ means convergence to zero in $P_{n,0}$-probability. We set
$\log0=-\infty$; the finite-valued expansion entails
$P_{n,0}(L_{n,h}=0)\to0$. Convergence in distribution is as in
[[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], and $N_d(0,K)$ allows
singular $K$ ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

If $P_{n,h}=\bar P_{n,h}$, this is the usual dominated LAN comparison. The
proxy formulation also covers QMD paths whose local alternatives are not
absolutely continuous with respect to the base law, provided the singular
product mass tends to zero in total variation. This definition is pointwise
in each fixed $h$; it does not assert uniformity over bounded sets of $h$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume AC and a parametric model QMD at $\theta_0$ with score $s_{\theta_0}$.
Then
$$E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}=0,$$
and the information matrix
$I_{\theta_0}=E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$ has finite entries
and is positive semidefinite. The QMD convention and square-integrability of
the score are those of [[def-qmd-path]].

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be one measurable space and let $P_n,Q_n$ be
probability measures on it ([[def-probability-measure]]). The sequence
$(Q_n)$ is **contiguous with respect to** $(P_n)$, written $Q_n\triangleleft
P_n$, if for every sequence $A_n\in\mathcal A$,
$$P_n(A_n)\longrightarrow0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q_n(A_n)\longrightarrow0.$$
The sequences are **mutually contiguous**, written $Q_n\triangleleft\triangleright
P_n$, if both $Q_n\triangleleft P_n$ and $P_n\triangleleft Q_n$.

Contiguity is a relation between sequences of laws, not absolute continuity at
each finite $n$. It says that events negligible under one sequence remain
negligible under the other in the indicated direction.

For each $n$, let $P_n,Q_n$ be probability measures on one measurable space,
and let $L_n\ge0$ satisfy $Q_n(A)=\int_A L_n\,dP_n$ for every measurable
$A$. Suppose $E_{P_n}L_n=1$, $L_n\Rightarrow L$ under $P_n$, $L\ge0$, and
$E L=1$. Then $(Q_n)$ is contiguous with respect to $(P_n)$.

derivations.claim: Let $A_n=\{1\}$. Then $P_n(A_n)=1/n\to0$, while $Q_n(A_n)=1/2$ for every $n$. By [F1], this disproves $Q_n\triangleleft P_n$.

On the two atoms, the density is $L_n(1)=\frac{Q_n\{1\}}{P_n\{1\}}=\frac n2,\qquad L_n(0)=\frac{Q_n\{0\}}{P_n\{0\}}=\frac{n}{2(n-1)}.$ Under $P_n$, the value $n/2$ occurs with probability $1/n$ and the other value tends to $1/2$, so $L_n\Rightarrow 1/2$. Each $E_{P_n}L_n=1$, but $E(1/2)=1/2\ne1$; hence the matching-mean condition of [F2] fails.

At the atom 1, the event probability under Pn is 1/n and under Qn is one-half. The singleton event is precisely the witness in step 1.1, not an irrelevant dimension boundary.

The limiting likelihood variable is the constant one-half, so its law is degenerate. Step 2.1 computes that its mean is below one despite each finite likelihood having mean one, explaining the failed sufficient hypothesis.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

Let $P_{n,h}$ be probability laws on a common measurable space for each
integer $n\ge1$ and local parameter $h\in\mathbb R^d$, where $d<\infty$ and
$P_{n,0}$ is the base law. Suppose that for every fixed $h$ we are supplied a
nonnegative measurable function $L_{n,h}$ with
$$\int L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}=1.$$
It defines an absolutely continuous proxy
$$\bar P_{n,h}(A):=\int_A L_{n,h}\,dP_{n,0}.$$
The actual local law is allowed to have a singular part; the approximation
condition below is what connects it to this proxy.

The experiments are **locally asymptotically normal (LAN)** at $h=0$ with
information matrix $K$ and central sequence $\Delta_n$ if $K$ is a symmetric
positive semidefinite $d\times d$ matrix, $\Delta_n$ is an $\mathbb R^d$-valued
statistic,
$$\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)\quad\text{under }P_{n,0},$$
and for every fixed $h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\|P_{n,h}-\bar P_{n,h}\|_{\rm TV}\to0,\qquad \log L_{n,h}=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TKh+o_{P_{n,0}}(1),$$
where $\|\cdot\|_{\rm TV}$ is the event-supremum total variation distance
([[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]) and
$o_{P_{n,0}}(1)$ means convergence to zero in $P_{n,0}$-probability. We set
$\log0=-\infty$; the finite-valued expansion entails
$P_{n,0}(L_{n,h}=0)\to0$. Convergence in distribution is as in
[[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], and $N_d(0,K)$ allows
singular $K$ ([[def-multivariate-normal-law]]).

If $P_{n,h}=\bar P_{n,h}$, this is the usual dominated LAN comparison. The
proxy formulation also covers QMD paths whose local alternatives are not
absolutely continuous with respect to the base law, provided the singular
product mass tends to zero in total variation. This definition is pointwise
in each fixed $h$; it does not assert uniformity over bounded sets of $h$.

In a local experiment $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ at $h=0$
([[def-lan-experiment]]), let $T_n$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued statistic.
It is **regular at zero with limit law $W$** if, for every fixed
$h\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$T_n-h\Rightarrow W\quad\text{under }P_{n,h},$$
where the same probability law $W$ works for all $h$. In a parametric model
with true parameter $\theta_0$, this is the definition for
$T_n=\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ and local laws at
$\theta_0+h/\sqrt n$; equivalently the centered error
$\sqrt n(\widehat\theta_n-\theta_0-h/\sqrt n)$ has a limit independent of
the fixed local displacement $h$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subseteq
\mathbb R^d\}$ be dominated by a common sigma-finite measure, with $\Theta$
open, and suppose the model is QMD at an interior $\theta_0$ with score $s$
and information $I=E_{\theta_0}[ss^T]$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID
$P_{\theta_0}$, and for each fixed local sequence $h_n\to h$ set
$u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$. Then the local product laws
$P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}$ admit mean-one likelihood-ratio proxies
$L_n$ relative to $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$ such that
$$\left\|P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}-L_nP_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\rm TV} \to0,$$
and under $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad \Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)\Rightarrow N_d(0,I).$$
Thus the IID QMD experiment is LAN in the proxy sense of
[[def-lan-experiment]]. This assertion does not claim that the full local
product law has a Radon–Nikodym derivative relative to the base law.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

derivations.claim: Let $g_\theta(x)=\sqrt{\phi(x-\theta)} =(2\pi)^{-1/4}e^{-(x-\theta)^2/4}$. By [F6] its derivative is $\partial_\theta g_\theta(x)=\tfrac12(x-\theta)g_\theta(x)$, so $\partial_\theta g_0(x)=\tfrac12xg_0(x)$. For $|\theta|\le1$, $|\partial_\theta g_\theta(x)| \le C(1+|x|)e^{-((|x|-1)_+)^2/4}=:G(x),$ whose square is integrable: it is bounded on $[-2,2]$, and for $|x|\ge2$ it is bounded by $C'(1+x^2)e^{-x^2/8}$. Substituting $x=2y$ reduces the tail integral to a constant times $\int(1+4y^2)e^{-y^2/2}dy$, finite by the second moment statement in [F2]. By [F7], $(g_t-g_0)/t=\int_0^1\partial_\theta g_{rt}\,dr$; this converges pointwise to $\tfrac12xg_0$. Its difference is bounded by $2G$, so [F5] applied to the squared difference gives convergence in $L^2(dx)$. Thus the QMD residual has norm $o(|t|)$, which is exactly the scalar QMD condition.

The density ratio is $\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\phi(X_i-h/\sqrt n)}{\phi(X_i)} =\exp\!\left(\frac h{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i-\frac{h^2}{2}\right).$ Each density is positive, so this is a full mean-one likelihood ratio. By [F2]–[F4], the characteristic function of $\Delta_n$ is $\prod_{i=1}^n\exp\left(-\frac{t^2}{2n}\right)=e^{-t^2/2},$ so $\Delta_n\sim N(0,1)$ exactly. Comparing with [F9] proves exact LAN with $K=1$ and no remainder.

The score is $s(x)=x$. By [F2], $E_0s=0$ and $E_0s^2=1$, so the information is $I=1$. By [F10], the general QMD-to-LAN result applies and predicts the same score and information; the direct computation below also shows the proxy is the exact alternative law.

Under $P_{n,h}$, the variables $X_i-h/\sqrt n$ are IID $N(0,1)$. The same characteristic-function product using [F3]–[F4] gives $\sqrt n\left(\bar X_n-\frac h{\sqrt n}\right) =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_i(X_i-h/\sqrt n)\sim N(0,1)$ exactly, which implies the displayed convergence. The limiting law does not depend on fixed $h$, which is regularity by [F9]. The calculation includes $h=0$ and every finite $h$.
